title: Humanistic Buddhism
hook: in Taiwan, movements bringing Buddhism into daily life, schools and hospitals

segments.voice: Yesterday, engaged in hard places: the hospice room, Angulimala's road, the practice of staying. Your line was in hard places. Who did you show up for? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

A monastery with a university next door. A temple with a clinic on the ground floor, a library, a cafeteria serving vegetarian lunch to office workers, a weekend class for children. On a Taiwanese hillside or in a city building, some Buddhist movements look less like a quiet retreat from the world and more like a small town built around kindness. That is on purpose. Their teachers say the Buddha's teaching belongs right in the middle of ordinary human life, at work, at school, in the hospital ward. Today: Humanistic Buddhism.
screen: `A TEMPLE WITH A CLINIC.` → `A SMALL TOWN OF KINDNESS.` → `ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: First, the name. In Chinese it is renjian fojiao, Buddhism in the human world. Its teachers say it is not a new school, just a way of putting the weight back where they believe it belongs: on the living, on this life, not mainly on funerals or on heavens far away. Second, the teacher behind it. In modern China, a monk named Taixu called for Buddhism to turn toward the living, to educate monks and nuns and to serve society. His student Yin Shun took that thread further, and when Buddhist teachers came to Taiwan, they carried it with them. Third, the text they lean on. Humanistic teachers point out that the Buddha was born, woke up and taught as a human being, among people. And they return to the old teaching that a human birth is hard to come by. The Dhammapada says it in a short verse which, put simply, runs: hard to win is a human life, hard to come by is hearing the teaching. If this life is that precious, they say, don't save your practice for later. Fourth, what it looks like. In Taiwan, large movements grew around teachers such as Master Hsing Yun of Fo Guang Shan and Master Sheng Yen of Dharma Drum Mountain. They built schools, universities and temples abroad, and taught that a kind word at work, an honest day's labor and a patient hour with your kids are all practice. Tomorrow we meet another, built around relief. Not every Buddhist puts the emphasis the same way. Some value retreat and renunciation more, and humanistic teachers would say those have their place too. But this movement's question is a simple one: if you have a human life today, what will you do with it?
screen: `BUDDHISM IN THE HUMAN WORLD.` · `TAIXU AND YIN SHUN.` · `A HUMAN BIRTH IS RARE.` · `SCHOOLS, HOSPITALS, WORKPLACES.` · then, large: `THIS HUMAN LIFE.`

segments.voice: Let the room you work in come to you, if you'd like to try this: a desk, a counter, a classroom, a kitchen at home. Settle the breath first. Then see the people in that room, one at a time. Let one face stay. Breathe in, and notice that they too have a human life, rare and brief. Breathe out, and choose one kind thing you could do for them today, something small and real. Hold it in mind. The bell holds the time.
Humanistic Buddhism. Buddhism in the human world: practice brought into daily life, schools, hospitals and work, because this human life is the place to practice. Today's word.
Your line: this human life. Today, do one kind thing at work, for the person you thought of, and let it count as practice. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Humanistic Buddhist movements, especially in Taiwan, run temples alongside schools, universities, hospitals and social services, and teach lay members to treat their work and family life as practice.

fork.reveal: Taixu called for Buddhism to turn toward the living. his student Yin Shun carried the idea further, and it took root in Taiwan.

what it means: Buddhism in the human world, practice brought into work, school and hospital.
what a scholar hears: renjian fojiao, a reform line from Taixu through Yin Shun, carried to Taiwan and built into large lay movements.
